text: Okapi BM25 is a probabilistic ranking function used by search engines to estimate the relevance of documents to a given search query. It is based on the probabilistic relevance framework developed in the 1970s and 1980s by Stephen Robertson, Karen Sparck Jones, and others. BM25 scores documents using term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length normalization. The formula includes two free parameters, k1 and b, that tune term frequency saturation and length normalization respectively. Typical values are k1 between 1.2 and 2.0 and b equal to 0.75. BM25 remains a strong baseline in information retrieval and is often hard to beat with more complex methods.

A cross-encoder jointly encodes a query and a candidate document into a single transformer model and outputs a relevance score. Unlike bi-encoders which embed query and document separately, cross-encoders use full attention across both inputs, giving much higher accuracy at the cost of speed. Because every query-document pair must pass through the model, cross-encoders are typically used only to re-rank a small set of top candidates retrieved by a faster first-stage retriever. Fine-tuning a cross-encoder on domain-specific query-document pairs substantially improves ranking quality for specialized corpora.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation, or RAG, combines a retriever with a language model. The retriever finds relevant passages from a knowledge base, then the generator conditions on those passages to produce an answer. RAG reduces hallucination by grounding the model in retrieved evidence and allows the knowledge base to be updated without retraining the model. A common architecture uses BM25 or dense embeddings for retrieval followed by a cross-encoder re-ranker, then a large language model for generation with citations.

FAISS is a library for efficient similarity search and clustering of dense vectors, developed by Facebook AI Research. It supports exact and approximate nearest neighbor search over millions of vectors. FAISS provides GPU acceleration and many index types including flat, IVF, HNSW, and PQ. For RAG systems, FAISS is commonly used to store document embeddings and retrieve the top-k most similar passages to a query embedding. Index choice trades off speed, memory, and recall.

LangChain is a framework for building applications powered by language models. It provides abstractions for prompts, chains, agents, memory, and tools. A chain composes multiple steps such as retrieval, prompt formatting, and model invocation. Agents use a language model to decide which tools to call and in what order. LangChain integrates with many vector stores, document loaders, and model providers. For RAG, LangChain offers a RetrievalQA chain that wires a retriever to a language model.

Text embeddings are dense vector representations of text produced by neural models such as sentence-transformers. Each piece of text is mapped to a high-dimensional vector such that semantically similar texts are close in vector space. Embeddings are compared using cosine similarity or dot product. For retrieval, document embeddings are precomputed and stored, while query embeddings are computed on the fly. Models like all-MiniLM-L6-v2 offer a strong balance of speed and quality for English retrieval.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) combines multiple ranked lists into a single ranking. For each document, it sums the reciprocal of its rank in each input list, weighted by a per-list weight. RRF is simple and surprisingly effective because it does not require calibrating incomparable raw scores across systems. It is commonly used to fuse sparse lexical retrieval like BM25 with dense neural retrieval. The standard RRF constant is 60, which controls how steeply rank contributions decay.

The Transformer architecture relies entirely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions. Self-attention allows each token to attend to all other tokens, capturing long-range dependencies. Multi-head attention runs several attention functions in parallel to attend to different representation subspaces. The scaled dot-product attention divides the query-key dot product by the square root of the dimension to stabilize gradients. Positional encodings inject order information into the otherwise permutation-invariant architecture.
